I liked the Odyssey. And now that it’s officially out of theaters, I want to talk about it (that’s not the real reason I waited this long, my writing schedule sucks). It’s always interesting when a large work like the Odyssey get’s adapted into a movie because in order to get the whole story into a sub three hour movie, you’ve got to leave a lot of the original source material on the cutting room floor. What’s cut and what’s left then tells you about what the director and writers are trying to say through the movie. Admittedly, this article is not really about my own thoughts on the movie, but tracing a particular theme through the movie and seeing how characters and scenes are used to develop it. Let’s jump in.

## Who are the people from the sea

In a movie so filled with individual themes (often tied to specific characters), it can be hard to pick just one to talk about. The first time I watched the movie, I thought I might write something about Odysseus and his internal struggle with needing to be in control and feel responsible for everything happening in his life. There’s also the subplot of Telemachus learning what it means to be a leader. But after rewatching, there is no doubt in my mind that the theme of violence toward the stranger is the primary one in Nolan’s Odyssey. And it’s tied most directly to this one phrase that is spoken throughout the movie: “The people from the sea”.

When the movie first opens, Telemachus is propelled on his journey to find news of Odysseus by the looming threat that a violent and irreverent people are sweeping across the mediterranean. Lawless power hungry people who can’t be reasoned with and can only be defended against. We hear this phrase again a little later as Odysseus and his crew first set out on their journey back home from Troy. On the first island they stop at (and really the only island where they don’t leave booking it on two feet), the villagers don’t welcome them because they think they’re “people from the sea”. Many other mentions are made of these people by various characters but they all paint the same picture.

Even when this specific phrase isn’t mentioned, the image it represents permeates the entire movie. The cyclops, the giant soldiers, even Calypso to an extent are all strangers who enact violence toward Odysseus and his crew and cannot be reasoned with (it’s only hinted at by thunder in the movie, but Calypso only let Odysseus go because sky daddy Zeus makes her). The moist poignant example of this is when Circe turns Odysseus’ men into pigs. Odysseus argues with her and asks “Did they hurt you?” and she says “They would have”. We are told by the opening of the movie that this is a world where Zeus’ law dictates that people be hospitable to strangers. But almost all we see are people being violent toward strangers. Everyone is so focused on their own wellbeing or grabs at power that it comes at the expense of kindness toward others. This theme really takes off though toward the end of the movie when Odysseus, disguised as a stranger, speaks to Penelope about the events of Troy.

## They’re all the people from the Sea

Years after the fall of Troy, finally home after a long suffered journey, Odysseus reflects aloud to Penelope on the night that won them the war. These events were now sung and celebrated through out the known world in song and verse, but he recounts them as nothing worth admiration. He tells of how they tricked the Trojans and used their own good will against them, giving them a gift of peace, only to stab them in the back and viciously burn their entire city down. They attack in the middle of the night, burning the city, killing men, women and children. Consider the sack of Troy from the perspective of the Trojans. Odysseus and his men are not the good guys. The Trojans are clad in all white armor while Agamemnon and his forces are draped in pitch black armor, Odysseus and his crew wearing suits only a shade or two lighter. Their “gift” for the goddess of wisdom is instead the deceit that destroys all decency. And for what? Agamemnon takes up the cause of Helen as an excuse to secure more power for their allied cities. This is not a just war.

After he finishes, Penelope cries and says “You’re the people from the sea”, to which Odysseus replies “Yes my Queen”. [^1] This is the big twist and a key that recontextualizes the entire movie. This whole time, the people from the sea have been some unknown threat, some other people who are lawless, unkind, almost inhumane. But at this point, we realize we’ve spent the entire movie with the people from the sea. Odysseus and his crew have sailed across the ocean, going from island to island. To the natives of those islands, they’re literally people from the sea. It’s ironic because in an area of connected islands like Greece, the only way to get from one island to the next is by sea. Every stranger is a person from the sea.

But the irony goes much deeper, because the entire movie, the suitors, people from Odysseus own homeland, have been acting in ways that typify “people from the sea”. They’re lawless, cruel to strangers, and seek only to gain power and position. Agamemnon came home and gave himself into the embrace of his wife, the furthest thing from a stranger, and is killed. Violence has spread everywhere and it’s because everyone is afraid of everyone. Everyone is plotting to get the better of everyone. How this plays out in human nature is said well by Thucydides, a disgraced Athenian general, when speaking on the revolution at Corcyra around 5th century BC:

> Thus every form of iniquity took root in the Hellenic countries by reason of the troubles. The ancient simplicity into which honour so largely entered was laughed down and disappeared; and society became divided into camps in which no man trusted his fellow. To put an end to this, there was neither promise to be depended upon, nor oath that could command respect; but all parties dwelling rather in their calculation upon the hopelessness of a permanent state of things, were more intent upon self-defence than capable of confidence.[^2]

The people who do respect Zeus’ law, like Telemachus and Odysseus’ sheep herd are trampled and spit on. Telemachus is attacked by fake priest in Athena’s own temple. No where is safe from the plotting and violence of men.

## We’re the people from the sea

Why spend time analyzing media like Nolan’s Odyssey? Perhaps because despite three thousand years of difference between us and the source material that Nolan’s adapted, the constancy of human nature has once again bridged our time to another’s. People will look back at this period of America’s history and speak of it as one characterized by divisiveness and inhospitality. We don’t speak to our neighbors. Either because we’re too busy or we can’t imagine that they have anything to offer us. We are uncharitable across the internet. Someone says something that we disagree with (or that we think we disagree with) and we flip. We read their words out of context and attack them. We say horrible things about what they’re like as a person (despite us knowing nothing about them personally other than a few of their opinions). The things I’ve mentioned aren’t physical, but they’re a form of social violence. And we do them for the same reason that people did in the Odyssey. We see that people have the potential to become obstacles to our flourishing and so we retaliate in advance.[^3]

We are good to who is good to us, because personal relationships and experience are held as the only lighthouses in a sea of nothingness. But what about the stranger? Or worse, the enemy? There is no reason or capacity to show them good. That is sad. Nonviolent movements around the world have shown that love for the stranger and the enemy is not only possible, but powerful.

That kind of love has the power to inspire real change. And yet we have no capacity in our current moment for that kind of love. Something has to change on that end, though I’m not sure what. However, I’m sure that If we make our posture one driven by self-defense and attack we will only hurt ourselves in the end. Because we too, to someone, are the people from the sea.\\

[^1]: There’s also a subtext of judgement from the gods on the men who participated in the siege of Troy. Agamemnon’s fate is the most obvious, but think about Odysseus and his crew. Even before they incur the curse of Poseidon by further injuring the Cyclops beyond what was necessary, the fact that they ended up at the Cyclops’ cave in the first place could be read as judgement. They must suffer someone who breaks the laws of Zeus and decency as those who have broken those laws themselves at Troy. All throughout the film Athena shows up at Odysseus’ side, shaking her head, offering small words of rebuke toward him. “Why don’t the god’s speak in ways we understand?” he says, to which she replies: “Who doesn’t understand pain, death, a good harvest”. In this rendition of the Odyssey, where the power and influence of the gods is more woven into the fabric of events than in personal confrontations, it’s not so hard to believe that Odysseus and his crew are under some period of testing or judgement. I’ve seen some mention that the movie ends on a weird note, since Odysseus’ is allowed to have the violent cathartic massacre of the suitors, but that this violence is condemned and so he is exiled, which can seem hypocritical. They needed the violence but it got him exiled. However, I think it is better to read this as just the semantic details of how the will of the gods is carried out. Odysseus is allowed by the gods to return home and have his vengeance, but he still must pay gravely for his part in the deception and massacre of Troy, an event that is framed as beginning the erosion of civility and as a result, civilization. This may be a stretch considering you might say Odysseus’ has already paid his due by being delayed from home for so long, but if his sin is as grave as he makes it out to be, then perhaps it is appropriate.

[^2]: Thucydides 3.70-85

[^3]: How we’ve gotten to this state is a little different. The postmodern view (developed after the modern age of “reason and civility” brought us two world wars and the development of weapons of mass destruction stronger and more deadly than the mythical gods of antiquity) persuades us that life is devoid of any common goodness. It says that we must create and secure our own wellbeing by whatever means necessary. Our current sliding moment, drifting more into what some call “meta-modernism”, oscillates between despair and hope, but overall, it’s proclivity toward absurdity and chaos brings us no closer to true hospitality.
